headings.title: Introduction to Fetal Circulation
headings.content: Before birth, the fetus lives in a liquid environment and does not use its lungs to breathe. Instead, the placenta acts as the baby's lungs, kidneys, and liver. Oxygen and nutrients are brought from the mother through the umbilical vein, while waste products are carried away through the umbilical arteries. Because the lungs are filled with fluid and do not take part in gas exchange, very little blood needs to flow through them. The fetal circulatory system is uniquely wired to bypass the lungs and liver, sending the richest, most oxygenated blood directly to the brain and heart.

headings.title: Key Fetal Shunts and Structures
headings.content:
To direct blood away from the unneeded organs, the fetal heart and blood vessels contain three special shortcuts called shunts:

1. **Ductus venosus**: A vessel that allows most of the oxygen-rich blood from the umbilical vein to bypass the liver and flow straight into the inferior vena cava.
2. **Foramen ovale**: A flap-like opening between the right and left atria that shunts blood directly into the left side of the heart, bypassing the lungs.
3. **Ductus arteriosus**: A muscular blood vessel connecting the pulmonary artery to the aorta, diverting remaining blood away from the lungs and into systemic circulation.

headings.title: The Trigger: First Breath and Cord Clamping
headings.content: Birth changes everything in a matter of seconds. When the newborn takes its first breath, the lungs expand, and air replaces the fluid inside the alveoli. This brings a rush of oxygen, which causes the tiny blood vessels in the lungs to relax and open up. At the exact same time, clamping the umbilical cord cuts off the low-resistance placental circuit. This sudden removal of the placenta causes a sharp rise in systemic blood pressure, flipping the pressure dynamics of the newborn heart.

headings.title: Pulmonary Vascular Resistance and Blood Flow Changes
headings.content:
Before birth, pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is extremely high because the blood vessels are squeezed shut in a fluid environment. Systemic vascular resistance is low because the placenta acts like a wide-open sponge. At birth, these pressures completely reverse.

- **Pulmonary resistance**: Drops dramatically as lungs expand and fill with oxygen.
- **Systemic resistance**: Increases significantly once the placenta is disconnected.

Because of these pressure changes, blood rushes into the pulmonary artery and floods the lungs to pick up oxygen, abandoning the old fetal pathways.

headings.title: Functional and Anatomical Closure of Fetal Shunts
headings.content: Once blood flow and pressure patterns reverse, the fetal shunts are no longer needed and begin to close. Functional closure happens first, driven by pressure changes and chemical signals. The foramen ovale slams shut because pressure in the left atrium becomes higher than in the right atrium. The ductus arteriosus and ductus venosus constrict and stop carrying blood shortly after birth. Over weeks and months, these functional closures turn into permanent anatomical structures, leaving behind fibrous remnants like the ligamentum arteriosum.

headings.title: Establishment of the Neonatal Circulation
headings.content: With the shunts closed and the lungs fully participating in gas exchange, the neonatal circulation matches that of an adult. Deoxygenated blood returns from the body to the right side of the heart, gets pumped through the pulmonary arteries to the lungs for oxygen, and returns to the left side of the heart. The left ventricle then pumps this freshly oxygenated blood out through the aorta to nourish the entire body. The transition is complete, and the baby is now successfully managing independent cardiorespiratory life.

headings.title: Clinical Implications of Delayed Transition
headings.content: Sometimes the smooth transition from fetal to neonatal circulation fails. If a baby suffers from birth asphyxia, cold stress, or severe respiratory distress, oxygen levels drop and blood vessels in the lungs stay tightly squeezed. This keeps pulmonary vascular resistance high and forces the newborn heart to keep using fetal pathways. Blood can continue to bypass the lungs through an open ductus arteriosus or foramen ovale, resulting in persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). Nurses must monitor vital signs, color, and oxygen saturation closely to catch these failing transitions early.
